title: Construction, Mechanics' Liens & New-Home Law
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: A mechanics' lien is best described as:
options: A lien against the contractor's personal assets only
A statutory lien against the improved property for unpaid labor or materials
A type of title insurance policy
A form of easement
rationales: It attaches to the property, not just the contractor's personal assets.
Correct. It is a statutory lien against the improved property.
It is unrelated to title insurance.
It is not an easement.

questions.stem: Parties who may file a mechanics' lien generally include:
options: Only the general contractor
General contractors, subcontractors, laborers, and material suppliers
Only licensed architects
Only the property's title company
rationales: Lien rights extend beyond only the general contractor.
Correct. Multiple tiers of contractors, laborers, and suppliers may qualify.
Architects are not the only eligible category.
Title companies do not file mechanics' liens.

questions.stem: A preliminary 20-day notice is significant because it:
options: Is optional and rarely used
Is generally required to preserve most claimants' future lien rights
Immediately creates a recorded lien
Only applies to general contractors with a direct owner contract
rationales: It is a required step for most claimants, not merely optional.
Correct. Serving this early notice generally preserves the right to later file a lien.
It preserves lien rights; it is not itself a recorded lien.
It is required especially for those without a direct owner contract, such as subcontractors and suppliers.

questions.stem: A homeowner pays the general contractor in full for a remodel. A subcontractor who was never paid by the general contractor then records a mechanics' lien. This is possible because:
options: The subcontractor's lien right runs against the property regardless of the owner's payment to the GC
Subcontractors can never file liens
The homeowner's payment automatically protects against all liens
Liens can only be filed by architects
rationales: Correct. Payment to the GC does not automatically protect the owner from a subcontractor's lien right.
Subcontractors are a recognized category of lien claimant.
Full payment to the GC does not automatically eliminate sub lien exposure.
Architects are not the only party who can file liens.

questions.stem: A practical risk-management step for homeowners undertaking significant construction is:
options: Avoiding any written contract with the contractor
Obtaining conditional lien releases tied to each payment stage
Paying the full contract amount upfront before any work begins
Ignoring subcontractor payment status entirely
rationales: A written contract is important, not something to avoid.
Correct. Conditional releases tied to payment stages help manage lien exposure.
Paying in full upfront increases risk rather than reducing it.
Ignoring subcontractor payment status increases lien exposure.

questions.stem: A conditional lien release differs from an unconditional release because a conditional release:
options: Is effective immediately upon signing regardless of payment
Is effective only once payment actually clears
Can never be used in California
Applies only to general contractors
rationales: That describes an unconditional release.
Correct. A conditional release protects against a payment that later fails to clear.
Conditional releases are a recognized, commonly used tool in California.
It can apply to subcontractors and suppliers as well as general contractors.

questions.stem: An unconditional lien release carries risk because:
options: It cannot be signed before payment
It is effective immediately upon signing, even if a payment check later bounces
It automatically voids the underlying contract
It is illegal in California
rationales: It can be signed before or after payment in various circumstances, which is part of the risk.
Correct. Signing it immediately releases lien rights regardless of whether payment later fails.
It does not void the underlying contract.
It is a legally recognized release type, not illegal.

questions.stem: Mechanics' lien priority is unusual because a lien can:
options: Never gain priority over a construction loan
Relate back to the commencement of work, potentially outranking a later-recorded but earlier-work-preceding construction loan
Only apply to commercial property
Automatically be junior to all recorded interests
rationales: Liens can, in specified circumstances, outrank certain later-recorded interests.
Correct. Relation-back to commencement of work is a distinctive and complex priority feature.
It applies to residential as well as commercial improvements.
Priority is not automatically junior; relation-back can change the analysis.

questions.stem: Construction lenders coordinate deed of trust recording timing carefully because:
options: Mechanics' lien relation-back rules can otherwise outrank the loan's priority
Recording timing has no effect on priority
Mechanics' liens are always junior to construction loans regardless of timing
Only owners need to worry about lien priority
rationales: Correct. Careful timing helps protect the lender's priority against relation-back mechanics' lien risk.
Recording timing has real priority consequences here.
Liens are not automatically junior; relation-back can change outcomes.
Lenders have a direct financial stake in this risk as well.

questions.stem: Mechanics' lien recording and foreclosure-filing deadlines are:
options: Flexible and rarely enforced
Strictly enforced statutory limits that can extinguish an otherwise valid claim if missed
Irrelevant to lien enforceability
Only applicable to commercial construction
rationales: They are strictly enforced, not flexible.
Correct. Missing these deadlines can extinguish an otherwise valid lien claim.
They are directly relevant to whether a lien can be enforced.
They apply broadly, not only to commercial construction.

questions.stem: California's Right to Repair Act primarily addresses:
options: Mechanics' lien filing deadlines
Statutory construction standards and a pre-litigation notice/repair process for new-home defect claims
Fair housing advertising rules
Escrow licensing
rationales: This is a separate topic from lien deadlines.
Correct. It establishes construction standards and a required notice/repair process before litigation.
It is unrelated to fair housing advertising.
It is unrelated to escrow licensing.

questions.stem: A buyer of a new home discovers a suspected foundation-related defect and wants to sue the builder. Under the Right to Repair framework, the buyer generally must first:
options: File suit immediately with no prior notice
Give the builder formal notice and an opportunity to inspect and attempt repair
Contact the original real estate agent to resolve it
Wait five years regardless of the defect's severity
rationales: Immediate suit without required notice can create procedural obstacles.
Correct. The pre-litigation notice-and-repair process is generally required before suing.
The selling agent is not the party positioned to resolve a construction defect claim.
There is no fixed universal five-year waiting rule described here.

questions.stem: Builder warranties on new construction typically:
options: Are identical for every system with no variation
Often have different coverage terms for different systems, such as shorter coverage for fixtures and longer for structural elements
Never exist in California
Replace the need for any statutory construction standards
rationales: Coverage often varies by system rather than being uniform.
Correct. Different systems commonly carry different warranty durations.
Builder warranties are a common feature of new-home sales.
Warranties are separate from, not a replacement for, statutory standards.

questions.stem: Unpermitted work is best understood as:
options: The same legal issue as a mechanics' lien
A separate risk affecting insurability, financing, and disclosure obligations
Always legal if the work looks professionally done
Irrelevant to a home sale
rationales: It is a related but legally distinct risk from mechanics' liens.
Correct. Unpermitted work carries its own insurability, financing, and disclosure consequences.
Appearance does not establish legality; permits and inspection sign-off are what matter.
It is highly relevant and must be considered in a sale.

questions.stem: A seller aware of unpermitted work completed years ago by a prior owner should:
options: Stay silent since it was not their own work
Disclose it as a known material fact
Only disclose if directly asked by the buyer
Assume it is irrelevant since time has passed
rationales: Knowledge, not who performed the work, triggers the disclosure duty.
Correct. Known unpermitted work is a material fact requiring disclosure.
The duty to disclose known material facts is affirmative, not conditioned on being asked.
Time passing does not eliminate the disclosure duty for known facts.

questions.stem: Retroactive permitting of previously unpermitted work can require:
options: No inspection at all
Exposure of the work for inspection, sometimes involving costly demolition
Immediate approval with no review
Only a verbal confirmation from the original contractor
rationales: Inspection is typically required, not waived.
Correct. Retroactive permitting can require exposing the work, which can be costly.
Review and inspection are typically required, not automatic approval.
A verbal confirmation alone is not a sufficient permitting process.

questions.stem: Joint checks or an escrow-style disbursement process on a large renovation project are used primarily to:
options: Speed up the contractor's personal profit
Help verify subcontractors and suppliers are actually being paid
Avoid the need for any lien releases
Eliminate the need for a written contract
rationales: This is not the primary purpose.
Correct. These mechanisms help ensure payment actually reaches subs and suppliers, reducing lien risk.
Lien releases remain important even with these mechanisms.
A written contract remains essential regardless of payment method.

questions.stem: An agent working with a client planning major renovations should flag mechanics' lien risk because:
options: It only matters to contractors, not clients
Owners can face lien exposure even after paying the general contractor in full
Liens cannot occur on residential property
It is entirely the escrow company's responsibility to explain
rationales: It directly matters to the owner's financial exposure.
Correct. Full payment to the GC does not eliminate sub/supplier lien risk.
Liens can and do occur on residential property.
Escrow is not typically involved in ongoing renovation payment structuring outside of a purchase transaction.
